explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…your hearts are filled with sorrow because I have told you these things.” (John 16:6) He also says none of them asks Him where He is going (John 16:5).
Not pride, friend. Jesus says their hearts are filled with sorrow because of what He told them (John 16:6). Sorrow is the word He picks. Pride never shows up in that verse.

Close, but Jesus doesn't call it doubt. He says, “…your hearts are filled with sorrow…” (John 16:6). Later in this same passage the disciples say, “…we believe that You came from God.” (John 16:30) So the word for this moment is sorrow, and I think a sad heart can go quiet like that.

explanations.answer: If He goes He will send the Advocate
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you.” (John 16:7) That's the benefit He's talking about. It sounds backwards at first, and I'd have squinted at it too.

explanations.answer: They will learn to lead on their own
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but Jesus never says that here. His reason is about the Advocate: “…if I go, I will send Him to you.” (John 16:7) The text doesn't tell us the disciples are being sent off to figure it out alone. They're getting help, and it's coming from Jesus.

explanations.answer: The world will stop hating them
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. At the end of this passage Jesus says, “In the world you will have tribulation.” (John 16:33) He ties the benefit to the Advocate, not to the world: “…if I go, I will send Him to you.” (John 16:7)

explanations.answer: They do not believe in Him
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says the Advocate will convict the world in regard to sin, “…because they do not believe in Me…” (John 16:9) He gives that reason and no other. Short and clear, just how I like my recipe cards.

explanations.answer: They have broken the Law of Moses
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason Jesus gives, friend. Moses and the Law don't come up in these verses. Jesus says the world is convicted in regard to sin “…because they do not believe in Me…” (John 16:9)
It sounds like it could fit, baker, but Jesus doesn't say it. The prophets don't come up in these verses. His reason is “…because they do not believe in Me…” (John 16:9)

Right, baker. Jesus says the Advocate will convict the world in regard to judgment, “…because the prince of this world has been condemned.” (John 16:11) That's the reason He gives. Three things on the list, and each one comes with its own because.
This one is true, friend. Jesus says the Advocate will convict the world in regard to judgment, “…because the prince of this world has been condemned.” (John 16:11) It's right there in the verse.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth.” (John 16:13) The disciples can't bear everything yet, so the Spirit does the guiding. A guide is a good thing to have when you can't carry the whole load at once.

Simon Peter, one of Jesus' disciples (John 13:6), is at the table that night. But Jesus doesn't name him as the guide. He says “…when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth.” (John 16:13) Peter is one of the ones being guided.
John the Baptist, who baptized Jesus (Mark 1:9), isn't in this conversation at all. The guide Jesus names is “…the Spirit of truth…” (John 16:13) He promises that He will guide them into all truth.
It's actually false, baker. Jesus says, “…He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears…” (John 16:13) The Spirit of truth speaks what He hears, and Jesus says so plainly.

That's correct, friend. Jesus says, “…He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears, and He will declare to you what is to come.” (John 16:13) So the Spirit speaks what He hears. No making it up as He goes.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.” (John 16:14) The Spirit takes what is Jesus' and shows it to them. All of it points back to Jesus.
Nope, baker. Jesus doesn't say the Spirit replaces Him. He says, “He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine…” (John 16:14) That's the opposite of a swap. This helper is there to show Jesus off.

Good guess, friend, but Jesus doesn't use that word. He says the Spirit “…will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.” (John 16:14) The work is taking what is His and showing it to the disciples. Defending isn't in the verse.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine.” (John 16:15) That's why He says the Spirit will take from what is His and disclose it. Everything the Father has belongs to Jesus.

Fun guess, friend, but angels aren't in this verse. Jesus says, “Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine.” (John 16:15) Only the Father gets named there. I've grabbed the wrong thing in my own bakery before, so I'm the last one to judge.

Prophets didn't sneak into this one, baker. I read the verse twice, which is two more times than I check my oven timer. Jesus says, “Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine.” (John 16:15) The Father is the One named, and that's the name that belongs in the blank.

explanations.answer: Ask one another what He means
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Some of His disciples “…asked one another…” what He meant, and then they kept asking (John 16:17-18). They say, “We do not understand what He is saying.” (John 16:18) It's a group chat with no answers, just everybody typing.

explanations.answer: Ask Jesus to say it plainly
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The disciples turn to each other: “Why is He saying, ‘a little while’? We do not understand what He is saying.” (John 16:18) They don't ask Jesus first. Verse 19 says He knew they wanted to question Him, and He spoke up.

explanations.answer: Keep quiet and wait it out
explanations.explanation: They don't keep quiet, baker. Some of the disciples asked one another, and “They kept asking…” (John 16:18) So waiting it out isn't what they do.
It's false, baker. John 16:19 says, “Aware that they wanted to question Him, Jesus said to them…” So He knew what they were wondering. Jesus already knew what they wanted to ask.

That's right, friend. Verse 19 says, “Aware that they wanted to question Him, Jesus said to them…” (John 16:19) He knew what was on their minds, and He brought it up Himself. They didn't even have to ask.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy.” (John 16:20) He says it right after telling them they will “…weep and wail…” Joy is the word He gives them.
Not anger, friend. Jesus says, “You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy.” (John 16:20) Anger doesn't come into this verse. He says their grief turns to joy.
No, baker. Jesus says they will “…weep and wail…” and then “…your grief will turn to joy.” (John 16:20) Their grief goes loud and then it turns to joy. Silence isn't the word He picks.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world.” (John 16:21) The joy is that big. Jesus uses her as a picture of how their grief will turn.

Not regrets, friend. Jesus says she “…forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world.” (John 16:21) Her joy is the whole point of the picture. Regret doesn't make it in.
That's not the word, baker. Jesus says the woman “…forgets her anguish…” (John 16:21) The word is forgets, and the reason He gives is her joy that a child has been born into the world.

True, baker. Jesus says, “So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.” (John 16:22) That's a joy nobody can take. I wish my cookie jar came with that promise.

It's true, friend, and I love this one. Jesus says, “…I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.” (John 16:22) That promise closes out the verse. Worth reading twice, baker.

explanations.answer: So their joy may be complete
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” (John 16:24) That's His reason for telling them to ask. Complete joy is the goal.

Not quite, friend. Jesus gives a different reason: “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” (John 16:24) The verse doesn't say anything about the world believing. The purpose He gives is that their joy may be complete.
That's a good guess, baker, but it isn't what Jesus says. He says, “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” (John 16:24) The reason He gives is their joy being complete.

explanations.answer: Tell them plainly about the Father
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, “An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you this way, but will tell you plainly about the Father.” (John 16:25) The figures of speech give way to plain talk. I think that's good news for anybody who's squinted at a hard saying.
No, friend. Jesus says He will “…tell you plainly about the Father.” (John 16:25) He's not quitting. He's changing how He talks.

explanations.answer: Speak to them only in dreams
explanations.explanation: Dreams aren't in this verse, baker. Jesus says the hour is coming when He will “…tell you plainly about the Father.” (John 16:25) Plain is the opposite of mysterious. No dream-reading required.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.” (John 16:27) The first blank is loved. The Father's own love is the one being talked about here.
That's right, friend. Jesus says they “…have believed that I came from God.” (John 16:27) That's the second blank. It sits right next to loved in the same verse.
Followed is a good word, baker, but it's not the one in this verse. Jesus says, “…because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.” (John 16:27) The words are loved and believed.
Served doesn't show up here, friend. Jesus says the Father loves them “…because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.” (John 16:27) Loved and believed are the two words.
Preached isn't in this verse, baker. Jesus says, “…because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.” (John 16:27) Those are the words that fill the blanks.

True, baker. The disciples say, “See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech.” (John 16:29) I bet they feel like they're finally getting it. I know that feeling, and it's a good one.

It's true, friend. The disciples say, “See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech.” (John 16:29) That's what they say right after Jesus says He came from the Father and will go back to Him. They say it's finally plain.

explanations.answer: Scatter and leave Him all alone
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker, and it's a heavy one. Jesus says, “…you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone.” (John 16:32) The same disciples who just said they believe will scatter. Jesus knew it, and He told them anyway.

explanations.answer: Stand beside Him to the end
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Jesus says, “…you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone.” (John 16:32) It's a hard thing to hear, and I think it was hard to say too.

Close, baker, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says they will be “…scattered, each to his own home…” (John 16:32) Scattered means going separate ways, not huddling together. It's a heavy part of the passage.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.” (John 16:32) The disciples will leave Him all alone, but He names the Father as the reason He isn't alone.
Good guess, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. His words are, “Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.” (John 16:32) The Father is the one He names.
That's not the reason Jesus gives, baker. He says, “Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.” (John 16:32) It's the Father He names, and nobody else.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” (John 16:33) He doesn't hide the trouble. He gives the reason for courage right after it. That kind of honesty is something I'd happily follow into any kitchen.

That's not what Jesus says, friend. He says, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” (John 16:33) He doesn't give a timeline for the trouble. His reason for courage is that He has overcome the world.

explanations.answer: The world will come to love them
explanations.explanation: No, baker. Jesus says, “In the world you will have tribulation.” (John 16:33) He never says the world will come to love them. His reason for courage is “I have overcome the world!” (John 16:33)
